claim: Mutations in the NRAS oncogene are present in up to 20% of melanoma.
source: Mutations in the NRAS oncogene are present in up to 20% of melanoma.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: IFI6 is necessary for NRASQ61K-induced transformation and melanoma growth.
source: Here, we show that interferon alpha-inducible protein 6 (IFI6) is necessary for NRASQ61K-induced transformation and melanoma growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soft agar assays and mouse tumor experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: IFI6 was transcriptionally upregulated by NRASQ61K.
source: IFI6 was transcriptionally upregulated by NRASQ61K
evidence: This is supported by gene expression array data and RT-qPCR results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown of IFI6 resulted in DNA replication stress due to dysregulated DNA replication via E2F2.
source: knockdown of IFI6 resulted in DNA replication stress due to dysregulated DNA replication via E2F2
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data, FACS analysis, and gene expression data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DNA replication stress consequentially inhibited cellular transformation and melanoma growth via senescence or apoptosis induction depending on the RB and p53 pathway status of the cells.
source: This stress consequentially inhibited cellular transformation and melanoma growth via senescence or apoptosis induction depending on the RB and p53 pathway status of the cells.
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining, annexin V staining, and cleaved caspase 3 immunoblotting shown in Figures 4, 7, and 8.

claim: NRAS-mutant melanoma were significantly more resistant to the cytotoxic effects of DNA replication stress-inducing drugs.
source: NRAS-mutant melanoma were significantly more resistant to the cytotoxic effects of DNA replication stress-inducing drugs
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9A comparing NRAS-mutant to BRAF-mutant, NF1-deficient, and triple wild-type melanomas.

claim: Knockdown of IFI6 increased sensitivity to DNA replication stress-inducing drugs.
source: knockdown of IFI6 increased sensitivity to these drugs
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of IFI6 expression by the MEK inhibitor trametinib, when combined with DNA replication stress-inducing drugs, blocked NRAS-mutant melanoma growth.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of IFI6 expression by the MEK inhibitor trametinib, when combined with DNA replication stress-inducing drugs, blocked NRAS-mutant melanoma growth.
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay and mouse tumor data shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, accounting for ~80% of skin cancer-related deaths.
source: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, accounting for ~80% of skin cancer-related deaths (Miller and Mihm, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miller and Mihm, 2006.

claim: Activating mutations of NRAS (typically NRASQ61K/R) occur in 20% of melanoma cases.
source: Some of the most commonly observed oncogenic events in melanoma are activating mutations of the oncogenic neuroblastoma RAS viral oncogene homolog (NRAS; typically NRASQ61K/R), which occur in 20% of cases (Miller and Mihm, 2006; Tsao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller and Mihm, 2006 and Tsao et al., 2012.

claim: Oncogenic NRAS causes constitutive activation of NRAS, resulting in activation of multiple downstream signaling pathways.
source: Oncogenic NRAS causes constitutive activation of NRAS, resulting in activation of multiple downstream signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Downward, 2003; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008; Wellbrock et al., 2004.

claim: Key pathways regulated by NRAS include the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and Ral guanine nucleotide dissociation stimulator (RalGDS) pathways.
source: Key pathways regulated by NRAS include the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and Ral guanine nucleotide dissociation stimulator (RalGDS) pathways, all of which are shown to play important roles in NRAS-driven oncogenesis (Downward, 2003; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Downward, 2003 and Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008.

claim: Inhibition of the PI3K pathway alone can result in compensatory upregulation of the MAPK pathway.
source: For example, inhibition of the PI3K pathway alone can result in compensatory upregulation of the MAPK pathway (Carracedo et al., 2008; Serra et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carracedo et al., 2008 and Serra et al., 2011.

claim: Targeting PI3K and MAPK pathways have not proven clinically beneficial for NRAS-mutant melanoma.
source: For this and several other known and unknown reasons, these approaches have not proven clinically beneficial (Baines et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baines et al., 2011.

claim: Gene expression analyses identified 301 genes that were significantly upregulated (p<0.05, fold-change >2.0) in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells compared to MEL-ST cells with an empty vector control.
source: Our gene expression data analyses identified 301 genes that were significantly upregulated (p<0.05, fold-change >2.0) in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells compared to MEL-ST cells with an empty vector control (Supplementary file 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IL8 and IL1B were among the top five upregulated genes and were previously implicated in RAS-mediated transformation.
source: Among the top five genes were IL8 and IL1B, which were previously implicated in RAS-mediated transformation (Cataisson et al., 2012; Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cataisson et al., 2012 and Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004.

claim: Three interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs)—IFI6, IFI27, and MX1—were identified that have not been previously implicated in oncogenic NRAS-induced transformation and melanoma tumor growth.
source: However, we also identified three interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs)—IFI6, IFI27, and MX1—that have not been previously implicated in oncogenic NRAS-induced transformation and melanoma tumor growth (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: IFI6 is overexpressed in melanoma samples.
source: Furthermore, an analysis of previously published melanoma datasets revealed that IFI6 is overexpressed in melanoma samples (Figure 1B–C) (Barretina et al., 2012; Haqq et al., 2005; Riker et al., 2008; Talantov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published datasets shown in Figure 1B-C and citations to Barretina et al., 2012; Haqq et al., 2005; Riker et al., 2008; Talantov et al., 2005.

claim: The MAPK pathway stimulated IFI6 expression effectively in MEL-ST cells.
source: Using these mutants, we found that the MAPK pathway stimulated IFI6 expression effectively in MEL-ST cells (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D-E using HRAS mutants that specifically activate MAPK or PI3K pathways.

claim: Introduction of MEK-DD in MEL-ST cells was sufficient to stimulate IFI6 expression.
source: To confirm this finding, we used the constitutively active MEK construct MEK-DD (Boehm et al., 2007) and found that the introduction of MEK-DD in MEL-ST cells was sufficient to stimulate IFI6 expression (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F-G and a citation to Boehm et al., 2007.

claim: IFI6 expression strongly correlated with the expression of other known MAPK transcriptional targets in patient-derived melanoma samples.
source: We observed that IFI6 expression strongly correlated with the expression of other known MAPK transcriptional targets (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of 20 patient-derived melanoma samples shown in Figure 1H.

claim: IFI6 overexpression significantly correlated with the NRAS mutation status in patient-derived melanoma samples.
source: Additionally, IFI6 overexpression significantly correlated with the NRAS mutation status in patient-derived melanoma samples (Figure 1I) (Haqq et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the Haqq melanoma dataset shown in Figure 1I and a citation to Haqq et al., 2005.

claim: BRAFV600E, similar to NRASQ61K, was able to activate IFI6 expression.
source: Our results showed that BRAFV600E, similar to NRASQ61K, was able to activate IFI6 expression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NF1 knockdown did not result in IFI6 upregulation.
source: However, NF1 knockdown did not result in IFI6 upregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells showed enrichment of NF-κB on the IFI6 promoter relative to MEL-ST cells expressing an empty vector.
source: MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells showed enrichment of NF-κB on the IFI6 promoter relative to MEL-ST cells expressing an empty vector (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: STAT1 was not enriched on the IFI6 promoter in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells relative to MEL-ST cells expressing an empty vector.
source: However, we did not observe enrichment for STAT1 on the IFI6 promoter in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells relative to MEL-ST cells expressing an empty vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: NF-κB knockdown markedly decreased IFI6 expression in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells.
source: We found that NF-κB knockdown markedly decreased IFI6 expression in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells (Figures 1L–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figures 1L-M and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: STAT1 knockdown had no effect on IFI6 expression.
source: whereas STAT1 knockdown had no effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Knockdown of IKKβ resulted in reduced phosphorylation of IκB.
source: Knockdown of IKKβ resulted in reduced phosphorylation of IκB (Figure 1—figure supplement 6)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: IKKβ knockdown resulted in reduced NF-κB reporter activity.
source: and reduced NF-κB reporter activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: IKKβ knockdown attenuated NRAS-induced IFI6 expression.
source: Analysis of IFI6 also revealed that IKKβ knockdown attenuated NRAS-induced IFI6 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: IKKβ knockdown resulted in decreased enrichment of NF-κB on the IFI6 promoter.
source: ChIP analysis showed decreased enrichment of NF-κB on the IFI6 promoter upon IKKβ knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: IFI6 knockdown inhibited the ability of NRASQ61K to transform MEL-ST cells, as shown by reduced colony formation in soft agar.
source: We found that IFI6 knockdown inhibited the ability of NRASQ61K to transform MEL-ST cells, as shown by the reduced colony formation in soft agar (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFI6 knockdown inhibited tumor formation in mice.
source: and tumor formation in mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant IFI6 ORF rescued growth both in soft agar and in mice.
source: Our results show that ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant IFI6 open reading frame (ORF) rescued growth both in soft agar and in mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NF-κB knockdown resulted in the inhibition of NRASQ61K-induced transformation.
source: Notably, NF-κB knockdown also resulted in the inhibition of NRASQ61K-induced transformation, further supporting a role for NF-κB in IFI6 expression (Figure 2D–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: shRNA-induced knockdown of IFI6 inhibited the ability of NRASQ61K mutant melanoma cells to form colonies in soft agar.
source: Our results show that shRNA-induced knockdown of IFI6 inhibited the ability of NRASQ61K mutant melanoma cells to form colonies in soft agar (Figures 3A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figures 3A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFI6 knockdown inhibited the ability of NRASQ61K mutant melanoma cells to form tumors in mice.
source: and to form tumors in mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IFI6 knockdown did not affect colony or tumor formation in YUVON cells.
source: However, IFI6 knockdown did not affect colony or tumor formation in YUVON cells (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR, soft agar, and mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant IFI6 ORF was able to rescue growth in both soft agar and in mice in YUGASP cells.
source: Our results show that ectopic expression of shRNA-resistant IFI6 open reading frame (ORF) was able to rescue growth in both soft agar and in mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The loss of IFI6 expression resulted in increased expression of transcription factor E2F2 and its target genes.
source: We found that the loss of IFI6 expression resulted in increased expression of transcription factor E2F2 and its target genes (Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by microarray and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many E2F2 target genes were previously documented to regulate DNA replication (e.g., CCNE1, MCM3, MCM10).
source: many of which were previously documented to regulate DNA replication (e.g., CCNE1, MCM3, MCM10) (Aladjem, 2007; Coverley et al., 2002; Thu and Bielinsky, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aladjem, 2007; Coverley et al., 2002; Thu and Bielinsky, 2013.

claim: Increased E2F2 protein level and increased E2F2 enrichment on the promoter of its target gene MCM10 were observed after IFI6 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, consistent with the increased level of E2F2 mRNA, we observed increased E2F2 protein level and increased E2F2 enrichment on the promoter of its target gene MCM10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of other E2F family genes in NRAS-mutant cells, MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells and primary human melanocytes after IFI6 knockdown revealed no changes in the expression of other E2F genes.
source: Analysis of other E2F family genes in NRAS-mutant cells, MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells and primary human melanocytes after IFI6 knockdown revealed no changes in the expression of other E2F genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: YUGASP cells expressing IFI6 shRNA displayed a significantly higher percentage of cells in S phase than the cells expressing NS shRNA.
source: YUGASP cells expressing IFI6 shRNA displayed a significantly higher percentage of cells in S phase than the cells expressing NS shRNA (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The loss of IFI6 resulted in dysregulated DNA replication, as observed by significantly fewer ongoing DNA replication forks, significantly more stalled forks, and a significantly higher number of newly fired origins of replication.
source: Our results showed that the loss of IFI6 resulted in dysregulated DNA replication, as observed by significantly fewer ongoing DNA replication forks, significantly more stalled forks, and a significantly higher number of newly fired origins of replication compared to melanoma cells expressing NS shRNA (Figures 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figures 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: IFI6 knockdown resulted in the accumulation of markers of cellular senescence.
source: IFI6 knockdown resulted in the accumulation of markers of cellular senescence (Figure 4E–G)
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: DNA replication stress-induced DNA damage was upregulated after IFI6 knockdown.
source: In addition, we also measured the phosphorylated histone γH2A.X as a marker of DNA damage, which showed that DNA replication stress-induced DNA damage was upregulated (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data for γH2A.X shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of E2F2 and IFI6 resulted in a significant rescue of the NRAS-mutant melanoma cell's ability to form tumors in mice.
source: and tumors in mice (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of E2F2 and IFI6 in melanoma cells resulted in a lower percentage of cells in S phase and normalized DNA replication compared with cells expressing IFI6 shRNA.
source: Furthermore, simultaneous knockdown of E2F2 and IFI6 in melanoma cells resulted in a lower percentage of cells in S phase and normalized DNA replication compared with cells expressing IFI6 shRNA (Figure 6A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 6A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of E2F2 and IFI6 prevented IFI6-induced senescence in melanoma cells.
source: We also evaluated senescence markers in this scenario and found that simultaneous knockdown of E2F2 and IFI6 prevented IFI6-induced senescence in melanoma cells (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The shRNA against E2F2 was highly specific to E2F2, as demonstrated by the unchanged mRNA levels of other E2F family genes.
source: The shRNA against E2F2 was highly specific to E2F2, as demonstrated by the unchanged mRNA levels of other E2F family genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Introduction of NRASQ61K in primary human melanocytes increased IFI6 expression and downregulated E2F2 and several E2F2 target genes.
source: Further studies revealed that the introduction of NRASQ61K in primary human melanocytes increased IFI6 expression and downregulated E2F2 and several E2F2 target genes, similar to melanoma cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of IFI6 in primary human melanocytes resulted in dysregulated DNA replication.
source: Additionally, knockdown of IFI6 in primary human melanocytes resulted in the dysregulated DNA replication (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFI6 knockdown in primary human melanocytes enhanced NRASQ61K-induced senescence.
source: Furthermore, IFI6 knockdown in primary human melanocytes enhanced NRASQ61K-induced senescence, as demonstrated by markers of cellular senescence (SA-β-gal and H2K9Ac) (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: An increase in γH2A.X was observed upon IFI6 knockdown in primary human melanocytes.
source: Consistent with our earlier results we observed an increase in γH2A.X upon IFI6 knockdown (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Expression of NRASQ61K resulted in increased IFI6 expression and decreased expression of E2F2 and its target genes in MEL-ST cells.
source: In complete agreement with our previous results, expression of NRASQ61K resulted in increased IFI6 expression and decreased expression of E2F2 and its target genes in MEL-ST cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Dysregulated DNA replication was observed in NRASQ61K-transformed MEL-ST cells expressing IFI6 shRNA.
source: We also observed dysregulated DNA replication in NRASQ61K-transformed MEL-ST cells expressing IFI6 shRNA (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Senescence induction was not observed in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells expressing IFI6 shRNA.
source: However, senescence induction was not observed in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells expressing IFI6 shRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of IFI6 in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells increased apoptosis under anchorage-independent growth conditions compared to NS shRNA-expressing cells.
source: We found that loss of IFI6 in MEL-ST/NRASQ61K cells increased apoptosis under anchorage-independent growth conditions compared to NS shRNA-expressing cells (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by GILA assay and poly-HEMA assay data shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: Apoptosis induction was confirmed by annexin V staining and immunoblot analysis of cleaved caspase 3.
source: We confirmed these results by annexin V staining and immunoblot analysis of cleaved caspase 3 (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This is supported by annexin V staining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: NRAS-mutant melanoma cells were significantly more resistant to the cytotoxic effects of DNA replication stress-inducing drugs compared to other genotypes (BRAF-mutant, NF1-deficient, or triple wild-type).
source: We found that NRAS-mutant melanoma cells were significantly more resistant to the cytotoxic effects of DNA replication stress-inducing drugs compared to other genotypes (BRAF-mutant, NF1-deficient, or triple wild-type) (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Knockdown of IFI6 sensitized NRAS-mutant cells to DNA replication stress-inducing agents.
source: Furthermore, we noted that the knockdown of IFI6 sensitized NRAS-mutant cells to DNA replication stress-inducing agents (Figure 9B)
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of both E2F2 and IFI6 rescued the effect of IFI6 knockdown on sensitivity to DNA replication stress-inducing agents.
source: and this effect was rescued by simultaneous knockdown of both E2F2 and IFI6 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Simultaneous treatment of NRAS-mutant cells with the MEK inhibitor trametinib and either hydroxyurea or aphidicolin resulted in significantly stronger melanoma growth inhibition in cell culture.
source: Remarkably, we found that simultaneous treatment of NRAS-mutant cells with the MEK inhibitor trametinib and either hydroxyurea or aphidicolin resulted in significantly stronger melanoma growth inhibition in cell culture (Figure 9C)
evidence: This is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Simultaneous treatment of NRAS-mutant cells with the MEK inhibitor trametinib and either hydroxyurea or aphidicolin resulted in significantly stronger melanoma growth inhibition in mice.
source: and in mice (Figure 9D)
evidence: This is supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: E2F2 and its target genes involved in the regulation of DNA replication were not upregulated in BRAF-mutant or NF1-deficient melanoma cell lines deficient in IFI6.
source: We did not observe similar changes in mRNA levels of E2F2 or its target genes after IFI6 knockdown in BRAF-mutant or NF1-deficient melanoma cell lines (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: ISGs play several important biological roles, including resisting and controlling pathogens.
source: ISGs are shown to play several important biological roles. Among these, their roles in resisting and controlling pathogens are well established (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schneider et al., 2014.

claim: In patients who respond to IFN-α-based treatment for HCV, expression of ISGs is low in the liver before treatment and increases significantly after treatment.
source: In patients who respond to this treatment, expression of ISGs is low in the liver before treatment and increases significantly after treatment (Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2008.

claim: Increased expression of 36 unique ISGs correlated with a reduction in HCV viral load.
source: Furthermore, increased expression of 36 unique ISGs correlated with a reduction in HCV viral load (Brodsky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brodsky et al., 2007.

claim: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) has been shown to use specific ISGs, such as RSAD2, to enhance infection.
source: It is important to note that some viruses, such as human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), have been shown to use specific ISGs, such as RSAD2, to enhance infection (Seo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seo et al., 2011.

claim: The introduction of oncogenic RAS into human cells induces responses similar to those seen during viral infections.
source: These results show that the introduction of oncogenic RAS into human cells induces responses similar to those seen during viral infections
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that oncogenic NRAS upregulates ISGs, which are typically induced during viral infections.

claim: Oncogenic NRAS uses ISGs, such as IFI6, to facilitate cellular transformation and tumor growth.
source: and oncogenic NRAS uses ISGs, such as IFI6, to facilitate cellular transformation and tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing IFI6 is necessary for NRASQ61K-induced transformation and melanoma growth.

claim: Some studies have shown that oncogenes induce DNA replication stress, resulting in cellular senescence.
source: Some studies have shown that oncogenes induce DNA replication stress, resulting in cellular senescence (Bartkova et al., 2006; Di Micco et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bartkova et al., 2006 and Di Micco et al., 2006.

claim: E2F transcription factors are downstream effectors of the retinoblastoma pathway, and their transcriptional activity is required to regulate various genes, including those required for DNA replication and cell cycle progression.
source: The E2F transcription factors are downstream effectors of the retinoblastoma pathway, and their transcriptional activity is required to regulate various genes, including those required for DNA replication and cell cycle progression (Bracken et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bracken et al., 2004.

claim: Context-specific roles for different E2F family members have been shown, which further highlights their non-redundant biological functions.
source: Context-specific roles for different E2F family members have been shown, which further highlights their non-redundant biological functions (Attwooll et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Attwooll et al., 2004.

claim: A number of growth inhibitory genes, such as CDKN2C (p18), CDKN2D (p19), CDKN1C (p57), E2F7, RB1 (pRB), and RBL1 are upregulated by E2F proteins during S phase.
source: Notably, although E2F family proteins are typically known to activate genes that facilitate cell cycle progression and proliferation, a number of growth inhibitory genes, such as CDKN2C (p18), CDKN2D (p19), CDKN1C (p57), E2F7, RB1 (pRB), and RBL1 are upregulated by E2F proteins during S phase (Di Stefano et al., 2003; Ortega et al., 2002; Sherr and Roberts, 1999; Stott et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Stefano et al., 2003; Ortega et al., 2002; Sherr and Roberts, 1999; Stott et al., 1998.

claim: None of the growth inhibitory targets of E2F were upregulated after IFI6 knockdown.
source: Interestingly, none of these growth inhibitory targets of E2F were upregulated after IFI6 knockdown
evidence: This is inferred from the microarray and RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multiple previous studies have demonstrated DNA damage in p53 and RB pathway-defective cells, resulting in p53- and RB-independent apoptosis.
source: Our results are consistent with multiple previous studies that have demonstrated DNA damage in p53 and RB pathway-defective cells, resulting in p53- and RB-independent apoptosis (Aladjem et al., 1998; Knudsen et al., 2000; Strasser et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aladjem et al., 1998; Knudsen et al., 2000; Strasser et al., 1994.

claim: Several agents such as aphidicolin, camptothecin, and hydroxyurea are used in clinical cancer treatment.
source: Several of the agents we used here, such as aphidicolin, camptothecin, and hydroxyurea, are used in clinical cancer treatment (Geyer and Mesa, 2014; Patel et al., 2006; Sargent et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geyer and Mesa, 2014; Patel et al., 2006; Sargent et al., 1996.

claim: These drugs will have limited utility in patients harboring NRAS and potentially other RAS mutations.
source: Based on our results, we speculate that these drugs will have limited utility in patients harboring NRAS and potentially other RAS mutations.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings that NRAS-mutant melanomas are resistant to DNA replication stress-inducing drugs.

claim: IKKβ was previously shown to be necessary for NF-κB activity and HRASv12-driven melanoma growth in mice.
source: IKKβ was previously shown to be necessary for NF-κB activity and HRASv12-driven melanoma growth in mice (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: The Talantov melanoma dataset analyzed 45 cutaneous melanomas, 18 benign melanocytic skin nevi, and 7 normal skin samples using Affymetrix U133A microarrays.
source: The Talantov melanoma dataset analyzed 45 cutaneous melanomas, 18 benign melanocytic skin nevi, and 7 normal skin samples using Affymetrix U133A microarrays.
evidence: This describes the composition of the Talantov dataset used for analysis.

claim: The Haqq melanoma dataset analyzed 25 melanomas, 9 non-neoplastic nevi, and 3 normal skin samples using a cDNA microarray.
source: The Haqq melanoma dataset analyzed 25 melanomas, 9 non-neoplastic nevi, and 3 normal skin samples using a cDNA microarray.
evidence: This describes the composition of the Haqq dataset used for analysis.

claim: The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) project is a compilation of gene expression data from 917 human cancer cell lines comprising 18 different tumor types.
source: The Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) project (i.e., Barretina cell line dataset) is a compilation of gene expression data from 917 human cancer cell lines comprising 18 different tumor types.
evidence: This describes the CCLE dataset used for analysis.

claim: The Riker melanoma dataset analyzed 40 metastatic melanomas, 42 primary skin cancers, 4 normal skin samples, and 1 normal skin primary cell culture using Affymetrix HG U133 Plus 2.0 microarrays.
source: The Riker melanoma dataset analyzed 40 metastatic melanomas, 42 primary skin cancers, 4 normal skin samples, and 1 normal skin primary cell culture using Affymetrix HG U133 Plus 2.0 microarrays.
evidence: This describes the composition of the Riker dataset used for analysis.

claim: All animal protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Yale University.
